rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a sharp story and a lawsuit-shaped hallucination. Its strongest line, "Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting," is aggressive but still anchored in legal threats and criticism. B has better nerve in places, especially "Does a publisher whose review drives a purchase share in the referral fee," but it poisons the set with "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" when the update says legal threats, not lawsuits. That is not spice; that is libel bait with a press-cardigan on.
gaps_in_A: A misses the sharper money-conflict inside the two launches: whether a cited publisher shares in referral fees, not just ad revenue. Its "One AI app, two new ways to take a cut" angle is clean but too polite.
"beyond subscriptions" imports a business-model reference not supplied in the update. Small leak, but the assignment was evidence-only.

The refusal of "The publisher-payout angle: how much will publishers actually earn?" is too absolute. With share terms or payout ranges, that becomes a legitimate accountability/data angle, not just a duplicate.
gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" invents a lawsuit. The update says criticism and legal threats. Those are not the same thing, and a media-business reporter will know it.
"settle out of court with product features" compounds the same problem. No active suit, settlement talks, or court posture appears in the facts.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer — and the publisher gets a slice of one payment" states the conclusion before proving the mechanism. B partly saves itself by admitting "if it is shared, this angle dies," but the headline already overclaims.

"A multi-billion-dollar valuation now has two revenue lines to defend it" is thin padding. B admits it is "a topic, not a story," which is the correct diagnosis and also the reason it should not be in the main set.
